lists.title: Hindi A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: First Hindi in communicative order: SOV word order, the three 'you's, होना, noun gender, plurals, postpositions, possession, the simple present, negation, questions, commands, and having things.

lists.title: Hindi A2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Building sentences: the oblique case, past था, the present continuous, the simple past, the ergative ने, the future, wanting/needing, सकना, comparisons, and the subjunctive.

lists.title: Hindi B1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Connected speech: compound verbs, the perfect tenses, three obligations, relative–correlatives, conditionals, the passive, manner adverbs, and experiencer subjects.

lists.title: Hindi B2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Nuance and control: causatives, the presumptive, aspect light-verbs, reported speech, participial phrases, and Hindi's irregular numbers.

lists.title: Hindi C1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Register and fluency: Sanskritic vs Perso-Arabic vocabulary, honorific concord, body-and-mind idioms, and discourse particles.

lists.title: Hindi C2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Mastery: ergative edge cases and split ergativity, and literary/poetic syntax with Urdu izāfat.

points.title: Word order: subject–object–verb
points.function: Build your first sentences — the verb goes LAST
points.explanation:
Hindi sentences put the verb at the end: **मैं सेब खाता हूँ** (I apple eat-am) = 'I eat an apple.' Everything else — time, place, objects — comes before the verb, usually in the order subject, time, place, object, verb.

There is no word for 'a' or 'the': किताब can mean 'a book' or 'the book' depending on context.
points.culture_note: Because the verb carries person and gender endings, Hindi often drops pronouns once the subject is clear — context does the work.

points.title: Pronouns and politeness: तू, तुम, आप
points.function: Choose the right 'you' for the person in front of you
points.explanation:
Hindi has three words for 'you':

- तू — intimate: small children, God, very close friends; easily rude
- तुम — informal: friends, younger people; takes plural-style verb forms
- आप — respectful: elders, strangers, teachers; takes plural verb forms

The other pronouns: मैं (I), हम (we), यह/ये (this/these, he/she nearby), वह/वे (that/those, he/she far).

Hindi has no separate 'he' vs 'she' — यह and वह cover both; the VERB ending shows gender.
points.culture_note: When in doubt, use आप. Using तू with a stranger is genuinely offensive, and many families use आप even with each other.

points.title: The verb 'to be': हूँ, है, हो, हैं
points.function: Say who or what someone is
points.explanation:
होना (to be) in the present:

| Person | Pronoun | Form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | मैं | हूँ |
| you, intimate | तू | है |
| he / she / it | यह / वह | है |
| you, informal | तुम | हो |
| we | हम | हैं |
| you, respectful | आप | हैं |
| they | ये / वे | हैं |

Unlike Russian or Arabic, Hindi NEVER drops the copula: 'I student' is wrong; you must say मैं छात्र हूँ.

The nasal marks matter: हूँ and हैं are nasalized, है is not.

points.title: Noun gender: masculine and feminine
points.function: Every noun has a gender — and the whole sentence agrees with it
points.explanation:
Every Hindi noun is masculine or feminine. Rules of thumb:

| Ending | Gender | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| -ा | usually masculine | लड़का boy, कमरा room |
| -ी | usually feminine | लड़की girl, कुर्सी chair |

But many nouns end in neither (घर house — masc., किताब book — fem., मेज़ table — fem.) and must be memorized with their gender.

Gender controls verb endings and adjective endings, so it is not decoration — खाता हूँ (male speaker) vs खाती हूँ (female speaker).
points.culture_note: Loanwords get genders too: ट्रेन (train) is feminine, फ़ोन masculine. Native speakers disagree about some recent loans.

references.title: Hindi: An Essential Grammar (McGregor, OUP outline)

points.title: Plurals: लड़के, लड़कियाँ, किताबें
points.function: Talk about more than one
points.explanation:
How a noun forms its plural depends on its gender and its ending:

| Noun type | Plural ending | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| masculine in -ा | -े | लड़का → लड़के, कमरा → कमरे |
| masculine, any other ending | unchanged | घर → घर |
| feminine in -ी | -ियाँ | लड़की → लड़कियाँ, कुर्सी → कुर्सियाँ |
| feminine, any other ending | -ें | किताब → किताबें, मेज़ → मेज़ें |

Adjectives and verbs agree: अच्छे लड़के (good boys), अच्छी लड़कियाँ (good girls).

drills.translation: There are four books on the table.
There are ten rooms in this building.

drills.hint: unmarked masculine — plural looks the same

points.title: Postpositions: में, पर, से, को
points.function: Say in, on, from, and to — AFTER the noun
points.explanation:
Where English has prepositions, Hindi has POSTpositions — they follow the noun: घर में (in the house), मेज़ पर (on the table), दिल्ली से (from Delhi), राम को (to Ram).

The big four: में (in), पर (on/at), से (from/with/by), को (to — marks the receiver, and specific objects).

The noun before a postposition changes to its oblique form — covered in its own lesson soon.

drills.translation: The book is on the table.
drills.hint: spatial postposition: contact with a surface, not enclosure inside it
spatial postposition: enclosure within a space, not contact with its top
postposition marking the source or origin point of the motion
the postposition of enclosed location, not a surface or a source

points.title: Possession: का, के, की
points.function: Say whose it is — and agree with the thing owned
points.explanation:
'X's Y' is X का/के/की Y. The form agrees with the thing OWNED (Y), not the owner:

| Form | The thing owned is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| का | masculine singular | राम का घर |
| के | masculine plural, or masculine singular before a postposition | राम के घर |
| की | feminine, singular or plural | राम की किताब |

Personal pronouns have their own forms: मेरा/मेरे/मेरी (my), हमारा (our), तुम्हारा (your), आपका (your — respectful), उसका (his/her), उनका (their).

drills.translation: Ram has two brothers. (Ram's two brothers)

points.title: Simple present: करता हूँ, करती है, करते हैं
points.function: Talk about habits and general truths
points.explanation:
The habitual present = verb stem + `ता`/`ती`/`ते` + the matching form of होना:

| Subject | Form |
| --- | --- |
| I, male | मैं खाता हूँ |
| I, female | मैं खाती हूँ |
| he | वह खाता है |
| she | वह खाती है |
| you, informal | तुम खाते हो |
| you, respectful | आप खाते हैं |
| we | हम खाते हैं |
| they, all female | वे खाती हैं |

The participle agrees in GENDER and NUMBER with the subject; होना agrees in person.

Use it for routines (मैं रोज़ चलता हूँ — I walk every day) and facts.

drills.sentence: मैं हर सुबह दौड़{{answer}} हूँ। (a man speaking)
drills.transliteration: main har subah daud{{answer}} hoon. (a man speaking)

drills.hint: habitual participle suffix - check the subject's gender
habitual participle suffix - let the subject's gender pick the vowel
habitual participle suffix - the subject's number AND gender both shape it

points.title: Negation: नहीं and मत
points.function: Say no, not, and don't
points.explanation:
Hindi has three negators:

- नहीं — the everyday 'not', right before the verb: मैं मांस नहीं खाता (I don't eat meat)
- मत — for negative commands: मत जाओ (don't go)
- ना — a softer 'don't', for polite requests and casual speech

In the habitual present the final होना is usually dropped under negation: वह नहीं आता (he doesn't come — no है needed).

points.title: Questions: क्या and the question words
points.function: Ask yes/no questions and information questions
points.explanation:
Sentence-initial क्या turns a statement into a yes/no question without changing word order: क्या आप चाय पीएँगे? (Will you have tea?). In speech, rising intonation alone also works.

The question words sit where the answer would sit (usually just before the verb): क्या (what), कौन (who), कहाँ (where), कब (when), क्यों (why), कैसा/कैसे (how), कितना (how much), कौन-सा (which).

drills.hint: interrogative asking for the identity of a thing, not a person
interrogative asking for a point in time
interrogative asking for a person's identity

points.title: Commands and requests: करो, कीजिए
points.function: Tell, ask, and politely request
points.explanation:
Each 'you' has its own command form.

तुम commands are stem + ओ: बैठो (sit), आओ (come), करो (do).

आप commands are stem + इए: बैठिए (please sit), कीजिए (please do), दीजिए (please give).

Four common आप forms are irregular: करना → कीजिए, देना → दीजिए, लेना → लीजिए, पीना → पीजिए.

Adding ज़रा (just/kindly) or कृपया (please, formal) softens further.

The bare stem is the तू command (बैठ!) — too blunt for learners to need.

points.title: Having things: के पास, का, को
points.function: Hindi has no verb 'to have' — here is what it uses instead
points.explanation:
Three constructions share the job:

- things you can pick up: X के पास Y है — मेरे पास एक गाड़ी है (I have a car; literally 'near me a car is')
- relatives and body parts: का/के/की — राम के दो भाई हैं (Ram has two brothers)
- states, feelings and illnesses: को — मुझे बुख़ार है (I have a fever; 'to-me fever is')

Choosing the right one is the whole lesson: possessions → के पास, relatives → का/के/की, states → को.

drills.translation: He has a lot of money.

drills.hint: relatives use the possessive — sister is feminine
an object you can hand over

points.title: The oblique case: कमरे में, लड़के को
points.function: Nouns change shape before postpositions
points.explanation:
Any noun directly followed by a postposition switches to its OBLIQUE form: कमरा → कमरे में (in the room), लड़का → लड़के को (to the boy).

| Noun type | Oblique singular | Oblique plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| masculine in -ा | लड़के को | लड़कों को |
| masculine, any other ending | घर में | घरों में |
| feminine | लड़की को | लड़कियों को |

Masculine -ा nouns take `-े` in the singular, and every plural takes `-ों` whatever the noun's type; feminine and unmarked singulars keep their direct form.

Adjectives and possessives shift too: मेरा → मेरे (मेरे घर में), बड़ा → बड़े (बड़े कमरे में).

drills.translation: We live in a big house.
drills.hint: house — unmarked masc., unchanged in singular

drills.translation: The book is in the room.
The teacher talks with the children.
There is no one in my house.

points.title: Past 'to be': था, थी, थे, थीं
points.function: Say how things were
points.explanation:
The past of होना agrees in gender and number:

| Gender | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| masculine | था | थे |
| feminine | थी | थीं |

The plural forms double as the respectful singular — थे for a man spoken to or about with respect (आप कहाँ थे?), and थीं for one respected woman.

In sentences: मैं वहाँ था (I was there — male), वह ख़ुश थी (she was happy), हम दोस्त थे (we were friends), वे अध्यापिकाएँ थीं (they were teachers — female).

Combine with the habitual participle for 'used to': मैं रोज़ दौड़ता था (I used to run every day).

drills.sentence: कल मैं घर पर {{answer}}। (a man speaking)
drills.transliteration: kal main ghar par {{answer}}. (a man speaking)

drills.translation: My grandmother was a teacher. (respect plural)
drills.hint: respected elders take the plural — feminine

points.title: Present continuous: रहा है, रही है, रहे हैं
points.function: Say what is happening right now
points.explanation: Stem + रहा/रही/रहे + होना: मैं खा रहा हूँ (I am eating — male), वह सो रही है (she is sleeping), हम पढ़ रहे हैं (we are studying). रहा agrees with the subject's gender and number; the stem never changes. The feminine marker रही covers both numbers, so it is होना that shows the number: लड़कियाँ खेल रही हैं (the girls are playing). Contrast with the habitual: मैं चाय पीता हूँ (I drink tea — in general) vs मैं चाय पी रहा हूँ (I am drinking tea — right now).

drills.sentence: मैं खाना बना {{answer}} हूँ। (a man speaking)
drills.transliteration: main khaana bana {{answer}} hoon. (a man speaking)

drills.hint: progressive auxiliary - inflect it for the subject noun's gender
progressive auxiliary - the subject's gender decides the ending

drills.sentence: मेरी माँ फ़ोन पर बात कर {{answer}} हैं।
drills.translation: My mother is talking on the phone.
drills.hint: progressive marker, feminine — with honorific हैं
drills.transliteration: meri maan fon par baat kar {{answer}} hain.

drills.hint: progressive auxiliary - agree with the subject in both number and gender

points.title: Simple past: गया, आई, पहुँचे
points.function: Say what happened — intransitive verbs first
points.explanation:
For verbs with no object (go, come, arrive, sleep), the perfective is the stem plus `-ा`, `-ी`, `-े` or `-ीं`, agreeing with the subject:

- masculine singular: वह गया (he went)
- feminine singular: वह गई (she went)
- masculine plural: हम आए (we came)
- feminine plural: वे पहुँचीं (they arrived — women)

Irregulars to memorize: जाना → गया, करना → किया, देना → दिया, लेना → लिया, पीना → पिया, होना → हुआ.

Transitive verbs work differently — the ने lesson is next, and this one sets it up.

drills.translation: The guests came in the evening.

drills.hint: happened — बारिश is feminine; होना is irregular

points.title: The ergative ने: मैंने किताब पढ़ी
points.function: Hindi's most famous trap — the verb agrees with the OBJECT
points.explanation:
With a TRANSITIVE verb in the perfective (completed) past, the subject takes ने and the verb agrees with the OBJECT, not the subject: मैंने किताब पढ़ी (I read the book — पढ़ी is feminine because किताब is feminine, regardless of who reads), राम ने आम खाया (Ram ate a mango — खाया masc. for आम).

The subject pronouns fuse with ने:

| Subject | With ने |
| --- | --- |
| मैं | मैंने |
| तुम | तुमने |
| आप | आपने |
| हम | हमने |
| वह | उसने |
| वे | उन्होंने |
| कौन | किसने |

If the object carries को, the verb gives up agreement and goes to neutral masculine singular: मैंने सीता को देखा (I saw Sita).
points.culture_note: This split-ergative pattern is shared with Punjabi, Gujarati and Marathi — mastering it in Hindi buys you three more languages.

drills.hint: ate — agrees with the mango, not Sita

points.title: Future: जाऊँगा, करेगी, मिलेंगे
points.function: Talk about tomorrow
points.explanation:
Future endings attach straight to the stem and agree in person AND gender — जाना right through:

| Person | Masculine | Feminine |
| --- | --- | --- |
| मैं | जाऊँगा | जाऊँगी |
| तू | जाएगा | जाएगी |
| वह | जाएगा | जाएगी |
| तुम | जाओगे | जाओगी |
| हम / वे | जाएँगे | जाएँगी |
| आप | जाएँगे | जाएँगी |

Every verb takes the same endings: वह करेगी (she will do), हम शाम को मिलेंगे (we will meet in the evening).

The form is the subjunctive plus गा/गी/गे, so the irregular subjunctives carry straight over: होना → होगा (will be), देना → देगा (will give), लेना → लेगा (will take).

drills.translation: I will go to Mumbai tomorrow. (male)
We will meet in the evening.
They will go to India next year.

points.title: Wanting and needing: चाहिए and चाहना
points.function: Ask for things two different ways
points.explanation: मुझे X चाहिए = 'I need/want X' (literally 'to-me X is-wanted') — the wanter takes को, and चाहिए never changes for tense in this basic use: मुझे पानी चाहिए (I want water), उसे मदद चाहिए (he needs help). With a verb: मुझे जाना चाहिए (I should go — infinitive + चाहिए gives advice). The full verb चाहना means to want/love: मैं सीखना चाहता हूँ (I want to learn), वह डॉक्टर बनना चाहती है (she wants to become a doctor).

drills.translation: I want a cup of tea.

drills.sentence: मैं हिंदी सीखना {{answer}} हूँ। (a man speaking)
drills.transliteration: main hindi seekhna {{answer}} hoon. (a man speaking)

drills.translation: We want to go to India.

points.title: Can and could: सकना
points.function: Say what you are able to do
points.explanation: सकना never stands alone — it follows a bare verb stem: मैं कर सकता हूँ (I can do), वह आ सकती है (she can come), हम जीत सकते हैं (we can win). Past: वह नहीं आ सका (he couldn't come). Future: मैं आ सकूँगा (I'll be able to come). Its cousin पाना suggests managing despite difficulty: मैं सो नहीं पाया (I couldn't manage to sleep).

drills.sentence: मैं हिंदी बोल {{answer}} हूँ। (a man speaking)
drills.transliteration: main hindi bol {{answer}} hoon. (a man speaking)

drills.sentence: मैं कल नहीं आ {{answer}}। (a man speaking)
drills.transliteration: main kal naheen aa {{answer}}. (a man speaking)

drills.sentence: बिना चश्मे के वह पढ़ नहीं {{answer}}।
drills.transliteration: bina chashme ke voh padh naheen {{answer}}.

points.title: Comparisons: से बड़ा, सबसे अच्छा
points.function: Compare things without 'more' or '-er'
points.explanation:
Hindi has no '-er' and no 'more': it compares with **से**. X, Y से बड़ा है = 'X is bigger than Y', literally 'X, from Y, is big'. The adjective has no comparative form of its own, but it still agrees with its noun: दिल्ली मुंबई से बड़ी है (Delhi is bigger than Mumbai — बड़ी is feminine for दिल्ली).

The superlative is सबसे, 'than all': सबसे अच्छा (the best), सबसे लंबी सड़क (the longest road).

ज़्यादा (more) and कम (less) step in where there is no adjective: मुझे चाय से ज़्यादा कॉफ़ी पसंद है (I like coffee more than tea).

drills.translation: An elephant is bigger than a horse.

drills.sentence: यह किताब उस किताब {{answer}} अच्छी है।
drills.translation: This book is better than that book.
drills.hint: postposition marking the standard the subject is measured against
drills.transliteration: yeh kitaab us kitaab {{answer}} achchhi hai.

points.title: Let's and may I: the subjunctive
points.function: Suggest, offer, and ask permission
points.explanation:
The subjunctive is the future minus गा/गी/गे: जाऊँगा → जाऊँ, चलेंगे → चलें, लूँगा → लूँ.

It does three jobs:

- suggestions and offers: चलें (let's go), बैठें (let's sit), चाय पिएँ? (shall we have tea?)
- permission: मैं आऊँ? (may I come?), क्या मैं यह लूँ? (may I take this?)
- after कि and ताकि, and after चाहना: मैं चाहता हूँ कि तुम आओ (I want you to come — literally 'I want that you come')

drills.hint: may I come — first person subjunctive

drills.sentence: मैं चाहता हूँ कि तुम रोज़ {{answer}}।
drills.translation: I want you to study every day.
drills.transliteration: main chaahtaa hoon ki tum roz {{answer}}.

points.title: Compound verbs: ले जाना, खा लेना
points.function: Add nuance — completion, suddenness, direction — with a light second verb
points.explanation:
A main verb stem plus a 'vector' verb adds aspect and colour:

- लेना — towards the doer, for one's own benefit: खा लेना (eat up), पढ़ लेना (read through)
- देना — away from the doer, for someone else: दे देना (give away), बता देना (tell)
- जाना — completion or change of state: सो जाना (fall asleep), मर जाना (die), आ जाना (turn up)
- डालना — doing it decisively or violently: कर डालना (get it done)
- बैठना — doing something you regret: कह बैठना (blurt it out)

जाना and आना keep their literal direction in the pair ले जाना (take away) and ले आना (bring).

Otherwise the vector loses its literal meaning, and the first verb stays a bare stem: खा लिया, never खाया लिया.

drills.translation: I ate up all the food.
The child fell asleep at once.
drills.hint: change of state — past of जाना

points.title: The perfect tenses: चुका है, गया था
points.function: Say what has happened and what had happened
points.explanation:
Three ways to say a thing is done:

- present perfect: perfective participle + the present of होना — वह आया है (he has come), मैंने खाया है (I have eaten)
- past perfect: the same participle + था, थी, थे or थीं — वह आया था (he had come)
- 'already done': stem + चुकना — मैं खा चुका हूँ (I have already eaten), फ़िल्म शुरू हो चुकी है (the film has already begun)

चुकना stresses completion, and its clause never takes ने even with a transitive verb: मैं खाना खा चुका हूँ, not मैंने. With था it gives 'had already': वह जा चुका था (he had already left).

drills.translation: I have seen this film before.

drills.translation: When I arrived, the train had already left.

points.title: Obligation: चाहिए, है, पड़ना
points.function: Three strengths of 'must' and 'have to'
points.explanation:
Three strengths of obligation, in rising order:

1. infinitive + चाहिए — should, ought: मुझे जाना चाहिए (I should go)
2. infinitive + होना — am to, it is arranged: मुझे कल जाना है (I have to go tomorrow)
3. infinitive + पड़ना — forced to by circumstance, no choice: मुझे जाना पड़ा (I had to go)

The subject takes को — मुझे, तुम्हें, उसे, हमें, आपको — and the infinitive agrees with the object: मुझे यह किताब पढ़नी है (पढ़नी is feminine for किताब).

drills.translation: You should go to the doctor.
I have to go to Delhi tomorrow.
We had to stop in the rain.
I have to take this medicine.
He has to get up early every day.

points.title: Relative–correlative: जो… वह, जब… तब
points.function: Join clauses the Hindi way — with matching pairs
points.explanation:
Hindi links clauses with paired words rather than a single 'which' or 'when': जो लड़का वहाँ खड़ा है, वह मेरा भाई है (the boy who is standing there is my brother).

| Relative | Correlative | Sense |
| --- | --- | --- |
| जो | वह | the one who, that which |
| जब | तब | when, then |
| जहाँ | वहाँ | where, there |
| जैसा | वैसा | as, so |
| जितना | उतना | as much as, that much |

जितना and जैसा change form like adjectives and the correlative matches them: जितने… उतने for a plural.

The जो-clause usually comes FIRST, and the correlative — वह, तब, वहाँ — picks it up in the main clause.

points.title: Conditionals: अगर… तो
points.function: Talk about ifs — real and imagined
points.explanation:
Conditions are built on **अगर … तो** (यदि is the formal अगर), and what the two clauses do with tense says whether the condition is real or imagined:

- real and open — future or present in both clauses: अगर बारिश होगी तो हम नहीं जाएँगे (if it rains, we won't go)
- unreal now — the imperfective `-ता` participle in both clauses: अगर मैं अमीर होता तो घर ख़रीदता (if I were rich, I would buy a house — but I'm not)
- unreal in the past — perfective participle + होता in the अगर-clause: अगर तुमने बताया होता तो मैं मदद करता (if you had told me, I would have helped)

तो ('then') opens the main clause and is often kept even when अगर is dropped.

points.title: The passive: खाया जाता है
points.function: Say something is done without naming the doer
points.explanation: Passive = perfective participle + जाना, conjugated for the tense: यहाँ हिंदी बोली जाती है (Hindi is spoken here), खाना बनाया जाता है (food is made), दरवाज़ा खोला गया (the door was opened), पत्र कल भेजा जाएगा (the letter will be sent tomorrow). The participle agrees with the grammatical subject: बोली is feminine for हिंदी, भेजा masculine for पत्र. The agent, if it is named at all, takes के द्वारा or से. The same shape with से expresses incapacity: मुझसे यह नहीं खाया जाता (I can't bring myself to eat this).

points.title: Adverbs and manner: से, कर के, तरह
points.function: Say how, and chain actions together
points.explanation:
Three constructions cover manner and chaining:

- से turns a noun into a manner adverb: ध्यान से (attentively), आराम से (comfortably), जल्दी से (quickly).
- The verb stem + कर (or के) is the conjunctive participle, 'having done…, then…': it chains actions that share one subject — खाना खाकर मैं सोया (having eaten, I slept), नहाकर वह गया (he bathed and left).
- की तरह means 'like' (शेर की तरह — like a lion), and के बारे में 'about'.

drills.translation: Having eaten, we went for a walk.
He is brave like a lion.
After bathing, he went to the office.

points.title: Experiencer subjects: मुझे लगता है, पसंद है
points.function: Feelings, opinions, and liking — the subject takes को
points.explanation: Many feeling/perception verbs make the experiencer take को (मुझे, तुम्हें, उसे…) and agree with the THING felt: मुझे यह पसंद है (I like this — 'to-me this is pleasing'), मुझे भूख लगी है (I'm hungry), मुझे लगता है कि… (I think that…), मुझे मालूम है (I know), उसे ग़ुस्सा आया (he got angry), मुझे हिंदी आती है (I know Hindi — 'Hindi comes to me'). What you like/know is the grammatical subject, so it drives the verb's gender and number.

points.title: Causatives: करना → कराना, बनना → बनाना
points.function: Say you got something done — by someone else
points.explanation:
Hindi builds causatives from one root in two steps. The direct causative inserts `-ा-` and makes you the one who acts: पढ़ना is to read, पढ़ाना to teach — to make someone read. The second causative inserts `-वा-` and puts an agent in between: पढ़वाना is to have someone taught, and that agent takes से — मैंने दर्ज़ी से कमीज़ सिलवाई (I had the tailor sew a shirt).

| Verb | Direct causative | Second causative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| बनना | बनाना | बनवाना |
| पढ़ना | पढ़ाना | पढ़वाना |
| उठना | उठाना | उठवाना |
| काटना | कटाना | कटवाना |
| करना | कराना | करवाना |
| खाना | खिलाना | खिलवाना |

Two adjustments recur: a long root vowel shortens before the suffix (काटना → कटाना, देखना → दिखाना), and a root that ends in a vowel takes `-ल-` (खाना → खिलाना, to feed; सोना → सुलाना, to put to sleep).

The teachers teach the children Hindi.

points.title: Presumptive: होगा, रहा होगा
points.function: Make educated guesses about now and the past
points.explanation: होगा/होगी/होंगे double as the presumptive ('probably is/will be'): वह घर पर होगा (he's probably home). Add participles for shaded guesses: वह सो रहा होगा (he must be sleeping — presumptive continuous), उसने खाया होगा (he must have eaten — presumptive perfect), वह रोज़ आता होगा (he probably comes daily — presumptive habitual). शायद (maybe) and ज़रूर (surely) tune the confidence.

points.title: Aspect verbs: लगना, रहना, चुकना, जाना
points.function: Say something began, kept on, or gradually became
points.explanation:
Beyond the simple tenses, a second verb marks aspect, and each one fixes the shape of the verb in front of it:

- लगना, after the oblique infinitive, means 'begin': वह रोने लगा (he began to cry), बारिश होने लगी (it began to rain).
- रहना, after a participle, means 'keep on': पढ़ता रहा (kept studying) with the imperfective, वह बैठा रहा (he remained seated) with the perfective.
- चुकना, after the bare stem, says the action is already over: वह खाना खा चुका है (he has already eaten).
- जाना, after the imperfective participle, marks gradual change: बड़ा होता जाता है (keeps getting bigger). After the perfective participle it means keeping on — the किए जाना pattern: वह बोले जा रहा था (he kept on talking).

drills.translation: The child suddenly began to cry.
The rain began to fall harder.
He kept studying till late at night.
People kept coming; the hall filled up.

drills.translation: He kept on talking without stopping.

points.title: Reported speech and कि-clauses
points.function: Report what people said and thought
points.explanation:
Hindi reports speech with **कि**, but it does not move the tense the way English does: the clause keeps the tense the words had when they were spoken.

The pronoun often stays unshifted too, so the report reads as a near-direct quote: उसने कहा कि मैं आऊँगा (he said he would come — literally 'he said that I will come'). Shifting it is ordinary as well: राम ने कहा कि वह थका है (Ram said that he was tired — 'he is tired', the present he spoke in).

कि also follows verbs of thinking, knowing, hoping and fearing: मुझे डर है कि… (I'm afraid that…), मुझे उम्मीद है कि… (I hope that…).

points.title: Participial phrases: आते हुए, बैठे-बैठे
points.function: Add rich 'while/-ing' description
points.explanation:
The imperfective participle + हुए means 'while -ing': घर आते हुए मैंने उसे देखा (while coming home, I saw him), मुस्कुराते हुए (smilingly).

The perfective participle + हुआ describes a resulting state: कुर्सी पर बैठा हुआ आदमी (a man seated on a chair), मेज़ पर रखी हुई किताबें (books lying on the table), थका हुआ (tired).

Doubling a participle stresses duration: बैठे-बैठे थक गया (got tired just from sitting), सोचते-सोचते (while pondering on and on).

The participles that modify a noun agree with it in gender and number (बैठा हुआ आदमी, रखी हुई किताबें), while the adverbial 'while -ing' phrase usually stays frozen in -ते हुए whatever the subject's gender: वह मुस्कुराते हुए अंदर आई (she came in smiling).

points.title: Numbers, ordinals, and fractions
points.function: Handle Hindi's notoriously irregular counting
points.explanation: Hindi cardinals are irregular through 100 and must be learned in blocks (इक्कीस 21, उनतीस 29, इकतालीस 41…) — each ten's transition is unpredictable. Ordinals: पहला (1st), दूसरा (2nd), तीसरा (3rd), चौथा (4th), then number + वाँ (पाँचवाँ 5th, दसवाँ 10th). Fractions have special words: आधा (½), पौना (¾ / 'quarter to'), सवा (1¼), डेढ़ (1½), ढाई (2½). Telling time and money leans on these constantly: सवा तीन बजे (3:15), डेढ़ सौ (150).

I need half a kilo of sugar.
Give me one hundred fifty rupees. (150)

points.title: Register: तत्सम Sanskrit vs Perso-Arabic vocabulary
points.function: Read the room — शुद्ध हिंदी, everyday Hindustani, or Urdu-leaning speech
points.explanation:
Hindi–Urdu share a grammar but draw vocabulary from two wells. The Sanskritic (तत्सम) layer dominates formal, literary and governmental Hindi; the Perso-Arabic layer dominates everyday speech, poetry and Urdu.

| Meaning | Sanskritic | Perso-Arabic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| thanks | धन्यवाद | शुक्रिया |
| question | प्रश्न | सवाल |
| news | समाचार | ख़बर |
| book | पुस्तक | किताब |

A fluent speaker code-switches by audience: a news anchor says प्रश्न, a friend says सवाल. Everyday speech also reaches for English, which belongs to neither well — विद्यालय is the formal word for school, स्कूल the one people actually say. Choosing the wrong register sounds stilted or, conversely, too colloquial for the setting.
points.culture_note: The nuqta (ख़, ग़, ज़, फ़, क़) marks Perso-Arabic sounds; dropping it (खबर for ख़बर) is common in casual writing but changes the 'correct' pronunciation.

points.title: Honorific concord and pronoun avoidance
points.function: Show respect through grammar, not just word choice
points.explanation: Respect is grammaticalized. A single respected person takes PLURAL agreement throughout: पिताजी आए हैं (Father has come — plural आए/हैं for one person), गुरुजी क्या कहते हैं? Third-person respect uses वे/उन्होंने even for one person. Polished speech often AVOIDS direct pronouns for elders, using titles or teknonyms (आपकी तबियत कैसी है? rather than तुम). Over-respecting a peer can sound sarcastic; under-respecting an elder is a real offense. जी appended to names/words (जी हाँ, राम जी) and standalone जी signal deference.

points.title: Idiomatic body-and-mind expressions
points.function: Speak like a native — feelings that live in the liver, not the heart
points.explanation:
Fluent Hindi runs on fixed expressions that don't translate literally. A body part supplies the seat of the feeling:

- मन (mind/heart) drives desire and engagement: मेरा मन करता है (I feel like), मन लगना (to feel settled).
- दिल carries emotion: दिल टूटना (for a heart to break).
- सिर carries burdens: सिर पर सवार होना (to be obsessed with).

A few verbs — आना, लगना, पड़ना — build hundreds more: याद आना (to remember), नींद आना (to feel sleepy), काम आना (to be of use), हाथ लगना (to obtain).

The आना and लगना idioms mark the experiencer with को (मुझे याद आया, बच्चे को नींद आ गई); the ones built on a body part take a possessive instead (मेरा मन करता है, उसका मन नहीं लगा). Either way, they are non-negotiable for sounding natural.

points.title: Discourse particles: तो, ही, भी, न, वाला
points.function: Master the little words that carry all the attitude
points.explanation:
Untranslatable particles do heavy lifting.

- तो marks contrast or topic: मैं तो जा रहा हूँ (as for me, I'm going).
- ही is 'only, exactly, the very': आज ही (this very day), वही (that exact one).
- भी is 'also, even': मैं भी (me too), एक भी नहीं (not even one).
- न softens a command or seeks agreement: चलो न (come on), आप आएँगे न? (you'll come, right?).
- वाला forms 'the one that/who' and marks imminence: लाल वाली किताब (the red book), दूधवाला (the milkman), ट्रेन आने वाली है (the train is about to arrive).

वाला is the one of the five that inflects: वाला, वाली, वाले agree with the noun. Placement changes scope, so these reward careful ear-training.

points.title: Ne-construction edge cases and split ergativity
points.function: Handle the ergative's genuine exceptions like a native
points.explanation:
The ने rule has real exceptions that even heritage speakers slip on.

- A few transitive verbs never take ने at all: लाना, भूलना, बोलना. The verb then agrees with the subject — मैं किताब लाया (I brought a book, a man speaking), not मैंने किताब लाई. मिलना is often listed here too, but it is intransitive to begin with (मुझे किताब मिली), so ने was never on offer.
- A conjunct verb follows its light verb: बात करना takes ने and agrees with बात (मैंने बात की), while a conjunct on होना never does (मुझसे ग़लती हुई).
- When a को-marked object appears alongside ने, agreement switches off and the verb sits in the masculine singular: मैंने लड़कियों को देखा, not देखीं.
- A transitive verb under an intransitive vector loses ने with it: वह पूरी किताब पढ़ गया, माँ बच्चे को डाँट बैठी.

points.title: Literary and poetic syntax: inversion, ellipsis, Urdu izafat
points.function: Read ग़ज़ल, film lyrics, and high literature
points.explanation:
Elevated registers bend the everyday rules.

- Word order inverts for emphasis or metre: the verb may precede its subject, and objects front — सुना है लोगों से (I've heard from people…).
- The Persian izāfat (-e-) links noun to modifier in Urdu-heritage phrases: शमा-ए-महफ़िल (the gathering's flame), तर्ज़-ए-बयाँ (manner of expression). It does the work का does in ordinary Hindi.
- Verse drops what prose spells out — a postposition, or the copula after a negative: दिल है कि मानता नहीं, where prose would close with मानता नहीं है.
- Compound Persian and Sanskrit tatpuruṣa formations pack whole phrases into single words.

Comprehension here rests on recognizing when the standard grammar is being deliberately suspended.
points.culture_note: Bollywood lyrics are the mass-culture gateway to this register — a single film song can carry izāfat, inversion, and dropped copulas in one line.
